newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Former Sri Lanka leader gets state funeral.
newsitem.headline: Former Sri Lanka leader gets state funeral.

text.p: Sri Lanka buried on Monday its first executive president, Junius Richard Jayewardene, a leader known for transforming the nation's economy but failing to settle a bitter separatist rebellion by minority Tamils.
Jayewardene died on Friday aged 90 after a brief illness. He was given a state funeral, which was televised nationwide.

Crowds lined the streets to watch the funeral procession, while others gathered at a historic Buddhist temple in Kelaniya, a northern suburb of Colombo, close to a river where Jayewardene had asked to be cremated.
A helicopter dropped flower petals on the crowd, few of whom displayed outward signs of sorrow at his death.
Jayewardene, a devout Buddhist, had asked that his ashes be scattered in the Kelani river where legend has it the Buddha bathed during a visit to the Indian Ocean island.
The village of Kelaniya, on the banks of the Kelani river, was Jayewardene's home seat that he successfully contested to enter parliament in 1943.

"The man widely acknowledged to be modern Sri Lanka's most astute politician ... will go on his last journey more as a spiritualist than the master of real politik that he was," the state-owned Observer said in an editorial.
"With his patrician manner and his aristocratic ways, JR would have made a good Roman Emperor and the style and the age would have suited the man," it said.
Jayewardene, popularly known as "JR", ruled the island from 1977 to 1988 as prime minister and as its first executive president.
The government of President Chandrika Kumaratunga declared Monday a day of national mourning and public institutions flew the national flag at half mast.

Jayewardene's reputation as a strongman and one of South Asia's shrewdest leaders suffered after his mid-1980s efforts to settle Sri Lanka's ethnic conflict failed and Tamil rebels intensified their war, which still plagues the country.
After his retirement in 1989 from 50 years of political life, Jayewardene bore the brunt of criticism for the island's economic and political ills.
